transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Kim (Redwood SE), Roberto Diaz (Argentum - Head of ML), Emily Zhang (Argentum - Platform Eng), Marcus Lee (Argentum - CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Primary goal: understand unit economics (per-token) and whether Argentum should use Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployment for generative agent workflows.
- Key constraints: strict budget cap for first year ($120k), latency SLOs for low-latency inference on customer-facing features, and security (KMS + SOC2) requirements.
- Agreed: run a 48-hour hosted pilot (100k tokens/day) and share pricing/TCO for Dedicated reserved capacity options.

Topics:
- Per-token pricing and billing model (hosted)
- Dedicated reserved capacity pricing and burst policies
- Batching and caching levers (prefix caching, KV cache miss rates, continuous batching)
- Budget/forecast for 90 days and cost/per-inference calculations
- Security: KMS, SSO, audit logs, data residency

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, you should be able to see my screen in a sec. I'm Samir from Redwood. Leah is my solutions engineer. Roberto, Marcus, Emily, thanks for making time.
[00:07] Roberto: Yeah thanks, Samir. We had a quick agenda, primarily cost assumptions and which deployment path makes sense for us. We run a recommendation service and an agent orchestration product, so lots of tokens, sometimes spikes.
[00:15] Samir: Got it. Leah, do you want to kick off with architecture and cost levers?
[00:18] Leah: Sure. So high level, Redwood has Hosted which is pay-as-you-go per token and per-embedding, Dedicated which is reserved GPU capacity with predictable throughput, and Private which is our VPC/on-prem package for regulated environments. For cost controls, the main levers are batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization/model choice.
[00:33] Emily: Quick interrup- sorry, when you say per-token, is that like gross tokens or only generated tokens? How do you bill for prompts vs completions?
[00:38] Samir: Good question. Hosted billing counts input + output tokens. For embeddings we bill per embed unit. For Dedicated we typically negotiate committed throughput and a flat monthly fee plus a small per-token surcharge for overflow.
[00:49] Marcus: Overflow? Meaning bursts above the committed?
[00:51] Leah: Exactly. You have a committed baseline bandwidth — say 100 rps sustained — and bursts are either queued or billed as burst capacity. We can set autoscale policies or queueing with best-effort latency.
[01:02] Roberto: Ok. Our rough numbers: baseline 150k tokens/day, but spikes to 600k tokens/day on earnings days. Budget: target FY1 spend <$120k. We need sub-200ms median latency for the recommendation endpoint.
[01:16] Samir: That's helpful. Quick back-of-envelope: if you used Hosted and average cost was $0.0005 per token (example), 150k tokens/day -> ~75 USD/day -> ~27k/month -> ~330k/year, so that exceeds your FY1 budget. But batching and caching can drop effective token spend significantly.
[01:34] Emily: Wait, $0.0005 is that Redwood's sticker?
[01:36] Samir: Not exact; it's an example. We'll send exact hosted per-token tiers in the spreadsheet. But importantly, effective cost is tokens consumed at the model level; with prefix caching and user-session KV cache hit rates you only send what you must.
[01:49] Leah: Right — two levers here: prefix or prompt caching (if many users share initial context you avoid resending that), and KV cache / key-value reuse inside the model session to avoid regen. Continuous batching also packs multiple requests into one GPU run, amortizing per-token kernel overhead and lowering latency/cost.
[02:05] Marcus: Curious — how much does batching hurt latency? Our SLO is 200ms median.
[02:09] Leah: There's tradeoff. Micro-batching at 10-20ms adds small latency but can increase throughput. We can tune max batching window and target latency. For median 200ms it's feasible; worst-case tail latency can still be higher but we have routing policies and fallback to smaller batch sizes for priority traffic.
[02:25] Roberto: Also how about model choice? We were evaluating Llama 3 70B quantized vs an instruction-tuned 13B.
[02:30] Leah: Larger models increase per-token time and cost; quantization reduces GPU memory and can enable larger batches on cheaper hardware. For many recommendation prompts 13B with good prompt templates + caching gives similar quality at a fraction of cost. We'll include model-specific unit costs in the TCO.
[02:45] Emily: Can Dedicated help us hit the $120k budget?
[02:47] Samir: Potentially. With Dedicated, you commit to a monthly pool — that's typically cheaper per token if you're consistently high-volume. Example: a dedicated 8xA100 equivalent pool with 24/7 usage might cost X/month versus hosted. The key is utilization; if you sustain the load, Dedicated drives down unit cost. But there's an up-front and commit.
[03:03] Roberto: We expect sustained baseline and big spikes; do you support burst capacity without rearchitecting?
[03:07] Leah: Yes — you can configure burst policies. If you hit bursts beyond the dedicated pool, we can route overflow to hosted or to a burst pool (pay-as-you-go). That gives a hybrid model.
[03:15] Marcus: That hybrid thing sounds ideal — reserved for baseline, hosted for spikes. Does Redwood have auto-routing by cost/latency?
[03:20] Leah: Yes, smart routing rules can send traffic based on latency SLO, cost thresholds, or region. You can prioritize certain API keys or endpoints for lower-latency reserved capacity and route less-critical background workloads to hosted.
[03:30] Emily: About caching — you mentioned KV cache. We use vector DB for embeddings, but we also have session states. How does Redwood integrate with that?
[03:36] Leah: We integrate at two levels: you can keep an external vector DB for retrieval augmentation, and Redwood's runtime supports local KV cache for repeated prefix tokens and optimizes KV cache placement to reduce re-encode cost. Note — transcription sometimes shows 'KB cache' in our auto notes — that's a mis-transcription.
[03:50] Roberto: For budgeting I'd like to see cost per served recommendation. For example, if our average prompt+completion is 200 tokens and caching reduces effective to 120 tokens, what does that mean in dollars?
[03:59] Samir: We'll create a cost model: Inputs — tokens per request (prompt+response), KV cache hit rate, batching efficiency (tokens amortized), model choice cost multiplier. Output — $/served request and projected monthly.
[04:12] Marcus: Do you publish typical batching efficiency numbers? Like how many requests per batch or percent cost reduction?
[04:16] Leah: We publish profiles: for latency-sensitive endpoints you might see 1.1–1.2x improvement; for throughput-heavy endpoints with high batching windows you can get 2x–4x cost reduction. But it depends on request size distribution.
[04:28] Emily: Ok, practical step: we'll give Leah our token distribution samples and she will run an internal sim?
[04:33] Leah: Yes, please send a sample of 1k–5k real-ish requests (anonymized) and we'll simulate costs under Hosted vs Dedicated and different cache hit rates. We'll also model a hybrid where bursts go to hosted.
[04:44] Roberto: On security — we need KMS integration for key management, RBAC, SSO, and audit logs. Any data residency constraints?
[04:50] Samir: Redwood supports KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM options for Private), SAML SSO, RBAC in Console, and audit logs. For Private deployments you can have control plane in your VPC or on-prem and keep data residency. We'll share SOC 2, ISO docs.
[05:04] Marcus: Do we ever see token content stored unencrypted in logs? That's a compliance no-no for us.
[05:09] Leah: By default we redact sensitive fields in logs and you can configure retention. For full isolation Private is recommended. For Hosted, we offer configurable retention and encryption at rest/in transit.
[05:20] Roberto: Any gotchas on quantization or model accuracy? We can't afford a 5–10% drop in recommendation relevance.
[05:26] Leah: Quantization can introduce minor quality differences. Our Optimize toolkit suggests quant/profile per workload and recommends A/B evals. We can run evals on your prompt set to quantify delta.
[05:36] Samir: Enough on that — let's talk concrete numbers in the spreadsheet. For demo numbers, assume hosted 0.00045–0.0006 per token depending on model, Dedicated committed pool amortized to 0.0002–0.00035 equivalent per token at high utilization. These are illustrative.
[05:51] Emily: That range clarifies things. If Dedicated gets us to ~0.00025/token and we do 150k tokens/day sustained, that's ~37.5/day -> ~13.7k/month -> ~164k/year. Still a little over. But with caching and batching if we reduce effective tokens 2x then we're under 120k.
[06:10] Leah: Exactly — effective token rate is the key. If caching hits 40–60% and batching gives 1.5–2x efficiency, Dedicated becomes compelling. Otherwise Hosted pilot to measure real-world hit rates is safer.
[06:22] Roberto: For the pilot, how do we instrument cost signals? We need token-level cost and latency per route.
[06:28] Samir: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and per-API-key dashboards. We'll give access to the Console for the pilot and show how to set alerts when spend approaches thresholds.
[06:39] Marcus: Who signs the NDA/contract for a pilot? We have procurement constraints.
[06:42] Samir: We can do a short pilot agreement — Leah can share the standard pilot SoW. For procurement, we'll also provide the security package to speed review.
[06:51] Emily: A couple of nitty-gritty Qs: network egress costs if we go Dedicated in a cloud region vs Private on-prem?
[06:57] Leah: Network egress is billed by the cloud provider typically. For Dedicated we can deploy in your preferred region to reduce egress. For Private on-prem there's no cloud egress but you pay for local infra. We'll include notes in the TCO spreadsheet.
[07:10] Roberto: Great. Any competitor pitfalls we should know? For ex, with some vendors burst routing is manual or requires duplicate infra.
[07:16] Samir: Yes — we see customers migrating from managed endpoints where burst handling was clumsy. Redwood's hybrid routing and autoscale policies aim to avoid that. Competitors like Paperspace or managed SageMaker endpoints often require more ops.
[07:28] Emily: Can we get an example TCO row now?
[07:30] Samir: Quick off-the-cuff: Hosted at 0.0005/token * 150k tokens/day * 30 = $2,250/month -> 27k/year. (Note: this is illustrative and maybe miscalculated in call).
[07:48] Roberto: Ok that number seems off relative to earlier — I think we need the spreadsheet.
[07:51] Samir: Agreed, spreadsheet will clear it.
[07:53] Leah: Action items recap — I'll run the cost sim when you send sample requests, Samir will send pricing and SOC2 docs, and Emily will provide token estimate and expected peak qps.
[08:03] Roberto: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[08:06] Marcus: One last: what's the minimum contract for Dedicated?
[08:08] Samir: Typical is monthly with discounts for annual commit. Some enterprise deals require 3–6 month minimums, but we can be flexible for pilot customers.
[08:17] Emily: Thanks everyone. We'll aim to get sample anonymized traffic by 2026-08-04.
[08:22] Samir: Great. I'll follow up with the TCO spreadsheet and pilot SoW. Thanks, talk soon.

[End of recording]
